transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (Apex Head of ML), Carlos Ruiz (Apex Infra), Samantha Lee (Apex Product)

Summary (auto): Quick scoping to align on benchmark harness integration, what scripts Apex will provide, streaming vs non-streaming tests, success criteria for POC, and an initial timeline.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to focus today's call on the benchmark planning and how we'll integrate your load scripts into our harness, um, and confirm success criteria and timelines
[00:12] Priya: thanks Maya, yep, really high level we want to validate two things: first that latency at our 95th and 99th percentile is within our targets, and second that throughput scales with reserved capacity. also cost per 1k tokens is a factor, obviously
[00:28] Liam: awesome. can you share the baseline numbers? like current latency on your infra and target SLOs?
[00:33] Priya: sure, currently in our prod infra our 95th is around 420ms for single-turn chat, 99th about 1.2s, target for POC is 250ms 95th and under 600ms 99th for the critical low-latency flows. for batch embedding jobs we care about tokens/sec and total run time more than p99
[00:50] Carlos: and from infra side we need to make sure networking doesn't add variance, we have strict egress rules, so we'll likely run the harness from inside our VPC or via an approved bastion
[00:58] Maya: good, that maps to the two deployment modes we typically test: hosted API with a dedicated route for the POC, and a private deployment if you want the harness inside the VPC. for the harness integration we usually accept customer-provided request scripts, or we can wrap them into our runner, which is what Liam will show
[01:14] Liam: yep, quick note about the harness: it's a small python runner that can run streaming and non-streaming scenarios, it supports async concurrency and can replay your exact request traces. we prefer getting your scripts because that gives us representative token distributions and prompt shapes
[01:26] Samantha: we have both — a streaming client for our chat UI and a non-streaming batch generator for nightly jobs. the streaming path is the trickier one for us because it affects perceived latency and memory on the server side
[01:36] Liam: understood. streaming tests are a bit different: we measure time-to-first-byte, ongoing throughput, and connection churn. non-streaming is simpler — full response latency and tokens/sec. our harness can run both, but streaming tests require instrumenting the client to open up server-sent tokens, sometimes websocket emulation
[01:52] Priya: how do you handle prefix caching and KV cache in the benchmarks? we rely heavily on caching for multi-turn flows
[01:58] Liam: good question — we can enable KV cache in the runtime and run cold vs warm cache scenarios. typically we run 1) cold-starts where KV not populated, 2) warm-run with representative prefix hits, and 3) mixed traffic. we'll need your sample traces to model that correctly
[02:12] Carlos: ok, on the network front we can provide an EC2 bastion inside our test VPC and open TLS egress to the Redwood endpoint, or we can give an IP allowlist. what do you need?
[02:20] Maya: either works. if you want us to run tests from inside VPC, we can bring a private deployment package, but that takes more time — typically a week-plus for system install in your env. for the faster path, we run from our hosted infra but pin capacity and run cross-region tests to simulate your latencies
[02:37] Priya: timeline-wise we want results within three weeks. doable?
[02:40] Liam: yes for initial micro-benchmarks and a hosted-run we can show results in about 10 business days assuming we get scripts and access to token distribution. private deployment tests will push timeline by ~2 weeks for install and network verification
[02:53] Samantha: what about load profile? we have bursty traffic: peaks are short but frequent, roughly 1k concurrent streaming sessions at peak across region with per-session message rate of 0.2 msg/s
[03:06] Liam: okay we'll need to model both steady-state and spike tests; harness supports ramp-and-hold and spike patterns. also want to confirm your max input length and avg token count per request
[03:16] Priya: avg input 120 tokens, avg output 240 tokens for chat responses, max 2k tokens in the longer summarization flows. for embeddings, average document 3k tokens and we do batched embeddings of 8k tokens per call often
[03:29] Maya: that helps with instance sizing. for Dedicated we normally recommend starting with a 4-GPU pool for throughput tests when you have mixed streaming and batch workloads; we can model smaller config for cost comparison
[03:40] Carlos: can the harness simulate partial responses like we get from streaming where clients cancel mid-stream? we have cancellation rates around 12% which affects token billing
[03:48] Liam: yes, the runner can issue client cancels at configurable points and we capture partial token counts. we also capture per-request cost estimates in post-processing so you can see billable vs actual tokens
[03:59] Priya: on success criteria beyond latency, we also want stability: sub-1% error rate and no memory leaks under 6-hour run at 80% load
[04:08] Liam: we'll add an uptime/stability checklist: error-rate, connection resets, OOMs, and memory drift, and we'll surface these in the run report and in the console dashboards
[04:18] Samantha: are you measuring quality regressions? sometimes quantization or smaller model variants change output and product needs a basic quality gate
[04:24] Maya: yes we can plug in your eval prompts and scoring — Redwood Optimize can run simple quality checks comparing outputs between baseline and POC model variants. for the POC we'll do a small set of prompts (20–50) to detect obvious regressions
[04:36] Priya: good. technical question: will the harness allow us to specify per-route batching and quantization profiles? because some flows can tolerate 4-bit quantization but others cannot
[04:44] Liam: the harness will accept a per-route config file; we can apply different quantization profiles and batching settings per route and run comparative tests. we log latency/cost tradeoffs per config run
[04:55] Carlos: on security, we'll need SOC2 docs and details on KMS/HSM key management if we consider private deployment. also audit log format for compliance
[05:04] Maya: we'll send the security pack — SOC 2 type II, our KMS integration notes, and sample audit log schema. for private installs we support customer-managed KMS and we can export logs in JSON LEEF/CEF style for SIEMs
[05:18] Priya: perfect, thanks. next, can we align on specific benchmark scenarios? I'd suggest: 1) streaming steady-state at 500c and 1kc spikes, 2) non-streaming single-turn 95th/99th latency at 100rps, 3) batch embedding throughput test with mixed document sizes
[05:32] Liam: that aligns. we'll map them to harness workloads: streaming-ramp, non-streaming-latency, batch-throughput. we'll also run cold vs warm KV cache and cancellation scenarios.
[05:43] Samantha: what about metrics export? can we push raw telemetry to our prometheus/kafka?
[05:48] Liam: we can export to prometheus pushgateway for short runs, or stream logs to your kafka via an exporter in the private deployment. hosted runs we'll provide full run CSVs and dashboards export
[05:59] Priya: great. on responsibilities: Apex provides request scripts and SLO targets, Redwood provides harness and runs hosted tests unless we opt for private install. agreed?
[06:09] Maya: agreed. I'll recap in the follow-up email and attach the harness quickstart and the run plan template
[06:15] Priya: timeline check: we aim to start harness runs by 2026-04-06 and have an initial report by 2026-04-13. is that ok?
[06:22] Liam: yes, as long as we get the scripts by 2026-04-01 and network access requirements by 2026-04-02. we'll prioritize the streaming steady-state first
[06:31] Samantha: question — do you simulate user think-time between messages? our chat flow has around 8s average think-time
[06:36] Liam: yes that's parameterizable; we'll set per-session think-time and message rates so concurrency maps to active sessions properly
[06:43] Carlos: one more infra detail: our egress path goes through a proxy that rewrites TLS SNI and we've seen issues before; can the runner respect custom SNI or use IP pins?
[06:51] Liam: the runner can be configured with custom SNI and connect via IP if needed, though IP pinning reduces flexibility. we'll note that as a potential friction point for private deploys
[06:59] Maya: ok, let's surface risks: private install timeline, proxy/SNI potential network flakiness, and needing representative scripts. any other risks?
[07:07] Priya: model drift — if we compare to a different model than our baseline it can confound quality checks. we'll define baseline model versions in the run plan
[07:15] Maya: good point.
[07:17] Liam: for deliverables we'll provide: harness repo link, run plan template, initial micro-benchmark results, and full run report with latency/cost/quality sections
[07:26] Maya: thanks everyone. we'll capture action items and get the follow-up out today.
[07:30] Priya: thanks all.

End of transcript.
